subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 2
summary: A 15-question test on Year 9 Chapter 9: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, shape of distributions, centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.
body:
This test covers Chapter 9, Probability and statistics: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, the shape of data distributions, measures of centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a histogram, table of outcomes or tree diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 9 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the masses (kg) of 40 dogs seen at a vet clinic. How many dogs were in the class 5 to less than 10 kg?
questions.explanation: The bar from 5 to 10 reaches a height of 11. The neighbouring bar (10) is for the next class.
steps: Find the bar that starts at 5 and ends at 10.
Read its height on the frequency axis: 11.

mistakes.A: Step 1: that is the bar for 10 to less than 15. Find the bar that starts at 5.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 5 is a class boundary on the horizontal axis. Read the bar’s height on the frequency axis.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 35 adds every bar from 5 upwards. Read just the one bar from 5 to 10.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the masses (kg) of 40 dogs seen at a vet clinic, with class boundaries 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and frequencies 5, 11, 10, 8, 4, 2

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the ages at which 60 people in a club retired from work. Which word best describes the shape of the distribution?
questions.explanation: It is negatively skewed: most values are high and a long tail stretches left, towards the smaller values. Naming a skew after its peak instead of its tail is the usual slip.
steps: Look for the peak (or peaks) and for any long tail.
Here most values are high and a long tail stretches left, towards the smaller values, so it is negatively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the skew is named after the tail, not the peak. Here the long tail points left, to the smaller values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: one side has a long low tail, so the two halves are not mirror images.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is only one peak. Bimodal needs two clear peaks.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the ages at which 60 people in a club retired from work, with class boundaries 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70 and frequencies 2, 3, 6, 11, 21, 17

questions.prompt: The number of push-ups 7 friends did: 15, 22, 18, 30, 11, 26, 18. What is the median?
questions.explanation: In order: 11, 15, 18, 18, 22, 26, 30. The middle (4th) value is 18. Taking the middle of the unordered list gives 30, which is wrong.
steps: 7 values, so the median is the 4th: 18.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 30 is the middle of the list as written. Put the values in order first.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 20 is the mean (total ÷ 7). The median is the middle value of the ordered list.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 19 is the range (30 − 11). The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A café offers 4 main meals and 3 desserts. How many different main-and-dessert combinations are there?
questions.explanation: Every one of the 4 outcomes of the first step can pair with every one of the 3 outcomes of the second: 4 × 3 = 12. Adding (7) misses most of the pairs.
steps: Step 1 has 4 outcomes and step 2 has 3.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added 4 + 3. Each of the 4 first results pairs with each of the 3 second results, so multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 4 counts only the mains. Each main can go with any of the 3 desserts.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 4 × 4 uses the mains twice. There are only 3 desserts.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the heights (cm) of 32 sunflowers. How many were 180 cm or more?
questions.explanation: The bars from 180 upwards have heights 6 + 2 = 8. Using only the first of those bars (6) misses the rest.
steps: "180 or more" means every bar that starts at 180 or higher.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 6 is only the bar from 180 to 200. Every bar further right is also "180 or more".
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included the bar from 160 to 180. Start at the bar that begins at 180.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 24 counts the values LESS than 180. Add the bars from 180 upwards.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the heights (cm) of 32 sunflowers, with class boundaries 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200, 220 and frequencies 2, 5, 8, 9, 6, 2

questions.prompt: The points scored by a team in 8 games: 40, 46, 37, 30, 33, 21, 24, 28. Find the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: Ordered: 21, 24, 28, 30, 33, 37, 40, 46. Q1 = (24 + 28) ÷ 2 = 26 and Q3 = (37 + 40) ÷ 2 = 38.5, so IQR = 12.5. The range (25) uses the extremes instead.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 25 is the range (46 − 21). The IQR is Q3 − Q1.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 31.5 is the median of the whole set. The IQR is the difference between the quartiles.
mistakes.D: Step 2: each half has 4 values, so its median is the AVERAGE of its two middle values, not one of them.

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. The table shows all the outcomes. What is the probability of a tail AND a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Only (T, 5) and (T, 6) have a tail and a number greater than 4: 2 of the 12 cells, so P = 2/12 = 1/6. Counting T4 as well gives 3/12 = 1/4.
steps: Tail AND greater than 4: (T, 5) and (T, 6) — 2 cells.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 2/6 is the chance of a number greater than 4 on its own. You also need a tail — use the whole 12-cell table.
mistakes.B: Step 2: adding 1/2 + 1/3 is for "or", not "and". Count the cells that have both a tail and 5 or 6.
mistakes.C: Step 2: "greater than 4" means 5 or 6 only. 4 itself is not greater than 4.

questions.diagram_alt: A table with the coin (H, T) down the side and the die (1 to 6) across the top; the 12 cells show H1 to H6 and T1 to T6

questions.prompt: A spinner lands on blue with probability 0.3. It is spun twice. Use the tree diagram to find the probability that it lands on blue both times.
questions.explanation: Blue then blue: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09. Adding (0.6) would make two blues MORE likely than one, which can’t be right.
steps: Follow the path Blue then Blue.

mistakes.B: Step 2: along a path you multiply, not add: 0.3 × 0.3.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 0.3 is only the first spin. Both spins must be blue.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 0.3 × 0.7 is blue then NOT blue. Follow the blue–blue path.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram with Blue 0.3 and Not blue 0.7 at the first spin, and Blue 0.3 and Not blue 0.7 again after each

questions.prompt: In a country, most people live into their 70s, 80s or 90s, but a small number die young. A histogram of age at death would most likely be:

options.A: Positively skewed, with the mean greater than the median
options.B: Negatively skewed, with the mean less than the median
options.C: Negatively skewed, with the mean greater than the median
options.D: Symmetric, with the mean equal to the median

questions.explanation: Most ages are high and the few young deaths form a tail to the left (negative skew), which pulls the mean below the median. "Positive" names the shape after the pile, not the tail.
steps: Most values are high; the few low values form a long tail to the left: negatively skewed.
The tail pulls the mean towards it, so the mean is less than the median.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the few YOUNG ages form a tail to the left, towards the small values — that is negative skew.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the left tail pulls the mean DOWN, below the median.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a long tail of young ages on one side means it is not symmetric.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the scores of 25 students on a quiz out of 20. What percentage of them were 12 or more?
questions.explanation: 7 + 4 = 11 out of 25, and 11 ÷ 25 × 100 = 44%. Giving 11% forgets to divide by the total.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you used only one bar (7). Include every bar that is 12 or more.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 11 is the NUMBER of them. Divide by the total of 25 and multiply by 100.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included one bar too many. Check where "12 or more" starts and stops on the horizontal axis.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the scores of 25 students on a quiz out of 20, with class boundaries 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and frequencies 2, 4, 8, 7, 4

questions.prompt: 5 parcels (masses in kg) have a mean of 30. 4 of them are 28, 35, 22, 31. What is the last one?
questions.explanation: All 5 must total 30 × 5 = 150; the known ones total 116, so the last is 150 − 116 = 34. Guessing it equals the mean is the common slip.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the missing value does not have to equal the mean. Use total = mean × number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there are 5 values, so the total is 30 × 5, not 30 × 4.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is the mean of the 4 known values. Find the total needed for all 5.

questions.prompt: A jar has 4 lemon and 6 orange lollies. Two are taken without replacement. Use the tree diagram to find the probability of getting one of each flavour.
questions.explanation: L then O = 4/10 × 6/9 = 24/90 and O then L = 6/10 × 4/9 = 24/90, so P(one of each) = 48/90 = 8/15. Stopping after one path gives 4/15.

mistakes.A: Step 3: lemon-then-orange is only one way. Orange-then-lemon also gives one of each — add both paths.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2 × 4/10 × 6/10 is WITH replacement. Use the tree’s second-stage fractions out of 9.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 7/15 is the chance of the SAME flavour twice. Use the two mixed paths.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram for two lollies without replacement: first L 4/10 and O 6/10; after L, L 3/9 and O 6/9; after O, L 4/9 and O 5/9; outcomes LL, LO, OL, OO

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers are added. What is the probability that the sum is less than 5?
questions.explanation: Sums of 2, 3 and 4 fill 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 of the 36 cells, so P = 6/36 = 1/6. 3/11 treats the eleven sums as equally likely.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 3 of the 11 possible sums are less than 5, but the sums are not equally likely. Count the 36 cells.
mistakes.C: Step 2: there are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 cells, not just one cell for each sum.
mistakes.D: Step 1: "less than 5" does not include 5. Count only sums of 2, 3 and 4.

questions.prompt: The mean of 6 numbers is 15. One number is removed and the mean of the other 5 is 14. What number was removed?
questions.explanation: Old total = 15 × 6 = 90; new total = 14 × 5 = 70; so the removed number is 90 − 70 = 20. It was above 15, which is why the mean fell.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 1 is how much the mean fell. Use totals: 15 × 6 and 14 × 5.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the removed number is not the new mean. Subtract the totals.
mistakes.D: Step 2: adding the two means does not give a data value. Find old total − new total.

questions.prompt: The probability that Mai passes her driving test on the first attempt is 0.6. If she fails, the probability she passes on the second attempt is 0.8. Use the tree diagram to find the probability that she passes within two attempts.
questions.explanation: She passes on Pass (0.6) or on Fail then Pass (0.4 × 0.8 = 0.32), so P = 0.6 + 0.32 = 0.92. 0.32 forgets the first-time pass.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 0.6 × 0.8 multiplies two passes, but she only does a second test if she FAILS the first. Use the paths that end in a pass.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 0.6 + 0.8 adds a branch from the wrong stage. A probability can’t be more than 1.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 0.4 × 0.8 is only "fail then pass". Passing first time (0.6) also counts.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first attempt Pass 0.6 or Fail 0.4; only after Fail is there a second attempt, Pass 0.8 or Fail 0.2
